results.question: How many wrong password attempts does it take before smart lockout locks an account in a normal commercial tenant?
results.answer: 10 failed attempts (the default lockout threshold in Azure Public and 21Vianet tenants).
evidence: The default is 10 for Azure Public tenants
results.response:
Under default settings, a commercial (Azure Public) tenant triggers a lockout after 10 incorrect password entries. Azure US Government tenants use three failed attempts instead.[1]

Repeated bad passwords don't count the same way. Smart lockout tracks the last three bad password hashes, so entering the same bad password multiple times doesn't increment the lockout counter.[1]

The exact count can differ slightly in practice, because the total number of failed sign-in attempts allowed before an account is locked out will vary slightly from the configured lockout threshold.[1]

results.question: A user got locked out by smart lockout. If they reset their password with 'I forgot my password', do they still have to wait for the lockout to run out?
results.answer: No. Choosing 'I forgot my password' in SSPR resets the lockout duration to 0 seconds. With 'I know my password' the lockout timer keeps running.

If the user instead picks "I know my password," the timer keeps running. The user then needs to change their password or wait for the lockout to expire.

results.question: Do passwords of users synced with password hash sync expire in Entra ID?
results.answer: Not by default: for password hash synchronized users the Entra ID password expiration is set to never expire, so they can still sign in to Entra ID with an expired on-premises password unless the cloud password policy is enforced for synced users.
results.evidence: the Microsoft Entra ID password expiration is set to never expire
results.response:
By default, passwords for password hash sync users don't expire in Entra ID, though older tenants may differ. Entra ID's expiration for these users is set to never expire, so even after the on-premises AD DS password expires, users can still sign in to Microsoft Entra ID using the expired password.[1] Previously, the default was 90 days. However, for tenants created around spring 2021 or later, the default value is never expire.[2]

Key points for a helpdesk agent:

- **Where the password is checked matters.** When signing in to a domain-joined client device, authentication occurs in on-premises AD DS, so the on-premises AD DS password expiration applies. When signing in to the Azure portal or Microsoft 365, the Microsoft Entra ID password expiration policy applies.[1]
- **To enforce expiration in Entra ID,** enable the CloudPasswordPolicyForPasswordSyncedUsersEnabled option at the tenant level.[2] Run $OnPremSync = Get-MgDirectoryOnPremiseSynchronization[2] and then set $OnPremSync.Features.CloudPasswordPolicyForPasswordSyncedUsersEnabled = $true[2], then apply it with Update-MgDirectoryOnPremiseSynchronization. Users changing passwords from Entra ID also need password writeback enabled in Microsoft Entra Connect.[2]
- **To check the current setting,** there's no simple way to check this in the Azure portal. You must calculate it using values obtained from PowerShell.[2]

results.question: Which password reset policy applies to admin accounts, and can admins use security questions to reset?
results.answer: Administrators get a strong default two-gate policy that requires two pieces of authentication data (e.g. email, authenticator app, phone). It prohibits security questions and can't be changed.

results.answer: The default sign-in frequency is a rolling window of 90 days.

results.question: Why does Microsoft recommend blocking legacy authentication protocols?
results.answer: Legacy protocols don't support MFA; more than 97% of credential stuffing attacks and more than 99% of password spray attacks use legacy authentication.

Blocking these protocols shuts down those attack methods. According to Microsoft, these attacks would stop with basic authentication disabled or blocked.[1]

results.question: Is there a way to see what a Conditional Access policy would do before turning it on?
results.answer: Yes, report-only mode: policies are evaluated at sign-in but not enforced, so admins can assess impact. It doesn't work for policies scoped to User Actions.
results.evidence: Report-only mode is a policy state that lets administrators test
results.response:
Yes. You can use report-only mode and the What If tool.

**Report-only mode:** Report-only mode is a policy state that lets administrators test most Conditional Access policies before enabling them.[1] During sign-in, the policy is evaluated but not enforced, and results are logged in the Conditional Access and Report-only tabs of the Sign-in log details.[1] Results are logged in the Conditional Access and Report-only tabs of the sign-in log details. Possible outcomes include "Report-only: Failure," meaning the conditions matched but a grant or session control wasn't met, and "Report-only: Not applied," meaning the policy's conditions weren't met. Customers with an Azure Monitor subscription can monitor the impact of their Conditional Access policies using the Conditional Access insights workbook.[1]

**What If tool:** This simulates a sign-in without waiting for real users to sign in. You can find it in the Microsoft Entra admin center > Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies > What If.[2] Only policies that are enabled or in report-only mode are included in an evaluation run.[2] The report lists the policies that apply to the user and those that don't, along with the reason each one doesn't apply.

**Limitation:** The What If tool doesn't test for Conditional Access service dependencies.[2] Also, the What If API expects all sign-in parameters to be defined for the evaluation to provide the most accurate results.[3]

results.question: What kind of hardware OATH tokens does Entra ID support?
results.answer: OATH TOTP SHA-1 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds; secret keys are limited to 128 characters.
results.evidence: OATH TOTP SHA-1 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds
results.response:
Entra ID supports **OATH TOTP** hardware tokens and does not support OATH HOTP. OATH time-based one-time password (TOTP) is an open standard that specifies how one-time password (OTP) codes are generated, and Microsoft Entra ID doesn't support OATH HOTP, a different code generation standard.[1]

Specifically, the service accepts tokens that use SHA-1 or SHA-256 and change their codes on a fixed interval. Microsoft Entra ID supports the use of OATH-TOTP SHA-1 and SHA-256 tokens that refresh codes every 30 or 60 seconds.[1]

Tokens can come in two forms:
- **Preprogrammed tokens** ship with their seed already loaded. Hardware OATH tokens typically come with a secret key, or seed, preprogrammed in the token.[2]
- **Programmable tokens** don't have a seed, so you set one. These programmable hardware tokens can be set up using the secret key or seed obtained from the software token setup flow.[1]

If you upload keys through CSV, they must meet format rules. Secret keys are limited to 128 characters, which isn't compatible with some tokens. The secret key can only contain the characters a-z or A-Z and digits 2-7, and must be encoded in Base32.[2]

results.question: What happens to Conditional Access policies if Entra ID has an outage?
results.answer: The Backup Authentication Service takes over; resilience defaults are enabled for all policies by default, but it can't evaluate all conditions in real time.
results.evidence: By default, resilience defaults are enabled for all policies
results.response:
During an Entra ID outage, the Backup Authentication Service takes over, and its behavior depends on whether the user already has a session.

- **New sign-ins are blocked.** The backup service doesn't support new sessions or authentications by guest users.[1]
- **Existing sessions can continue.** When an existing session needs a new token, all Conditional Access policies are reevaluated. If there are no Conditional Access policies, or if all the required controls, such as MFA, were satisfied at the beginning of the session, the Backup Authentication Service issues a new access token to extend the session.[1]
- **Some conditions can't be rechecked.** If a policy's controls weren't satisfied earlier in the session, the policy is reevaluated, but not all conditions can be reevaluated in real time during an outage. These conditions include:[1] group membership, role membership, sign-in risk, user risk, country/region location, and authentication strengths (the list in the source[1]).
- **Resilience defaults decide the gap.** Conditional Access resilience defaults are a new session control that let admins decide between[1] blocking authentications whenever a policy condition can't be evaluated in real time, or allowing policies to be evaluated using data collected at the beginning of the user's session.[1]
- **Defaults are on.** Resilience defaults are automatically enabled for all new and existing policies. Microsoft recommends keeping the resilience defaults enabled to reduce the impact of an outage. Admins can disable resilience defaults for individual Conditional Access policies.[1]
- **Phishing-resistant requirements may not be enforced.** When active, the Backup Authentication Service doesn't evaluate authentication methods required by authentication strengths.[1] A user who signed in with a non-phishing-resistant method before the outage may not be prompted for MFA during it, even for a resource requiring phishing-resistant authentication.

The results don't say whether policies are changed or disabled during an outage, or how the service behaves beyond these cases.

sources.title: Resilience defaults for Microsoft Entra Conditional Access
quotes: If the primary authentication service is unavailable, the Microsoft Entra Backup Authentication Service automatically issues access tokens to applications for existing sessions. This functionality significantly improves Microsoft Entra resilience because reauthentications for existing sessions account for more than 90% of authentications to Microsoft Entra ID. The Backup Authentication Service doesn't support new sessions or authentications by guest users.

When an existing session expires during a Microsoft Entra outage, the request for a new access token routes to the Backup Authentication Service, and all Conditional Access policies are reevaluated. If there are no Conditional Access policies, or if all the required controls, such as MFA, were satisfied at the beginning of the session, the Backup Authentication Service issues a new access token to extend the session.

If the required controls of a policy weren't previously satisfied, the policy is reevaluated to determine whether access should be granted or denied. Not all conditions can be reevaluated in real time during an outage. These conditions include:

- Group membership
- Role membership
- Sign-in risk
- User risk
- Country/region location (resolving new IP or GPS coordinates)
- Authentication strengths

During an outage, the Backup Authentication Service can't evaluate all conditions in real time to determine whether a Conditional Access policy applies. Conditional Access resilience defaults are a new session control that let admins decide between:

- Whether to block authentications during an outage whenever a policy condition can’t be evaluated in real-time.
- Allow policies to be evaluated using data collected at the beginning of the user’s session.

Resilience defaults are automatically enabled for all new and existing policies. Microsoft recommends keeping the resilience defaults enabled to reduce the impact of an outage. Admins can disable resilience defaults for individual Conditional Access policies.

When active, the Backup Authentication Service doesn't evaluate authentication methods required by authentication strengths. If you used a non-phishing-resistant authentication method before an outage, during an outage you aren't prompted for multifactor authentication even if accessing a resource protected by a Conditional Access policy with a phishing-resistant authentication strength.

sources.title: Security questions authentication method
quotes: Security questions aren't used as an authentication method during a sign-in event. Instead, security questions can be used during the self-service password reset (SSPR) process to confirm who you are. Administrator accounts can't use security questions as verification method with SSPR.

Security questions are stored privately and securely on a user object in the directory and can only be answered by users during registration. There's no way for an administrator to read or modify a user's questions or answers.

Security questions will be retired for Self‑Service Password Reset (SSPR) in March 2027. After that date, users will no longer be able to reset passwords using security questions. Ensure users are set up with supported authentication methods in the Authentication methods policy.
This feature is being deprecated due to security risks and low reliability. Security questions are often guessable or susceptible to social engineering, increasing the risk of account takeover during SSPR. Stronger verification methods improve security and reduce reset failures and support escalations.
Prepare in advance to avoid user lockouts, helpdesk escalations, and failed password reset experiences once enforcement begins in March 2027.
